H&P – Super Detailed Note

Consult Summary:
54-year-old male with untreated hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and smoking history presented via video consultation with sudden-onset, constant mid-sternal pressure-type chest discomfort of two hours’ duration radiating to the left shoulder/arm, associated with dyspnoea, light-headedness, and nausea; ambulance arranged for probable acute coronary syndrome.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Pressure in middle of chest like someone sitting on it,” began suddenly while digging in the garden ~2 h prior to call.  
• Severity: 7/10 at onset and currently; persistent, non-fluctuating.  
• Radiation: Left shoulder and arm. No radiation to head or back.  
• Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath (unchanged since onset), light-headedness, persistent nausea without vomiting, recent progressive exertional dyspnoea with calf pain and leg swelling on stair climbing/uphill walking.  
• Exacerbating/alleviating factors: Began with mild exertion; no relief at rest; no medications taken.  
• Review of systems (pertinent):
  – Cardiopulmonary: No palpitations reported.  
  – GI: Nausea; no vomiting; no dysphagia; normal bowel/urinary function.  
  – Neuro: No focal deficits.  
  – Musculoskeletal: Calf pain, leg swelling with exertion.  
  – No fever, cough, or recent infection reported.

Past Medical History:
• Hypertension – diagnosed, not on pharmacotherapy; complications not documented.  
• Hypercholesterolaemia – diagnosed, not on pharmacotherapy.  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• None currently taken (for HTN or lipids).  
• No other regular medicines disclosed.

Allergies:
• Drug allergies not documented (information incomplete).

Social History:
• Smoker; quantity and duration not specified.  
• Lives with wife at home; generally limited activity due to exertional dyspnoea; gardens fortnightly.  
• Alcohol and recreational drug use not discussed.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Remote visit; no vital signs or physical findings available.

Investigations:
• None performed prior to ambulance arrival; paramedics to obtain ECG, vital signs, and initiate hospital work-up.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute chest discomfort – suspicion of Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)  
  • Assessment: Sudden persistent pressure-type chest pain with left-arm radiation, autonomic symptoms, multiple cardiovascular risk factors.  
  • Plan:  
    – Emergency transfer via ambulance to nearest hospital (initiated).  
    – Paramedics to monitor vitals, obtain ECG, give oxygen and other acute management per protocol (doctor advised attachments to arms, breathing support).  
    – Hospital to provide immediate consultant review on arrival.  
    – Clinician to stay on phone until paramedics arrive; will arrange follow-up appointment post-hospitalisation.

Issue 2: Possible alternative diagnoses (e.g., pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection)  
  • Assessment: Dyspnoea, calf pain/leg swelling raise PE concern; abrupt pain warrants consideration of dissection.  
  • Plan: Hospital evaluation to include appropriate imaging/labs (e.g., D-dimer, CT angiography, bedside echocardiography) as determined by ED/consultant team.

Issue 3: Chronic cardiovascular risk factors – untreated hypertension and hyperlipidaemia; smoking  
  • Assessment: Long-standing risk factors likely contributing to current presentation.  
  • Plan: To be addressed after acute episode; clinician will schedule follow-up visit to initiate guideline-directed therapy and smoking cessation counselling.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina/NSTEMI) – High likelihood: Classic pressure pain, left-arm radiation, autonomic features, multiple risk factors.  
2. Pulmonary embolism – Moderate likelihood: Acute dyspnoea, chest discomfort, history of calf pain/leg swelling; needs exclusion.  
3. Aortic dissection – Low–Moderate likelihood: Sudden onset in hypertensive patient; pain quality less typical but must be ruled out.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing expected elements: vital signs, full medication list, drug allergies, family history, alcohol and substance use details.  
• Conflicts: None identified between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Good clarity; brief pauses and minor overlaps but history largely complete.
